column2: Sir, they say this must be sent in secret.
Did they tell you to announce that in the passage?
No sir. I saved that part for you.
Very considerate. Let me see what they've sent.
Sir, I've read the instructions three times. This one is for encoding.
Did the instructions require three readings?
No sir. I wanted to avoid having to come back.
Then we'll both appreciate it if the paper is in order.
Sir, I don't think the message says anything very interesting.
Were you asked for an opinion on it?
No sir. Only to bring it for encoding.
Let's confine ourselves to that task.
Outgoing message for your machine, sir.
The message is for me. I'll deal with the machine.
Sir, the radio watch says to bring back something they can transmit.
That depends on what you've brought me.
The message, sir. I haven't forgotten it.
Then you can let go of it now.
Sir, if this is secret, why is it written in plain language?
Because I haven't encoded it yet.
Of course, sir.
Give it here before you discover any more security problems.
Sir, I caught this before the ventilation carried it under a bunk.
Was it meant for the bunk?
No sir. Encoding and transmission.
Then the bunk can wait. Put it on my desk.
Sir, may I ask how the men ashore know what your letters mean?
They have their instructions.
The same as yours?
You have instructions too, sailor. What do they say?
To bring you this message for encoding, sir.
Let's begin with those.
Sir, I'm delivering this on behalf of the watch officer.
Are you asking on his behalf as well?
Only whether you can encode it, sir.
I can examine it. Approval comes after the examination.
Message for encoding, sir. Everything they gave me is here.
Good. I'll tell you if they should have given you more.
Sir, the hatch slammed behind me. I nearly dropped your message.
It isn't my message yet.
No sir. It's the one that needs encoding.
Let's keep it on the desk until it has stopped trying to escape.
Sir, this looks much worse than when I brought it in.
It's encoded. It isn't supposed to make sense to you.
Excellent work, then, sir. I haven't understood a word.
The radioman will be delighted. Take it to him.
Ready for transmission, sir?
Ready. Bring the papers to the radio watch.
Sir, should I tell the radioman how to read this?
He needs to transmit it, not read it for entertainment.
Yes sir. I was afraid he might ask me.
Tell him it's cleared. He knows his own work.
Sir, you turned an ordinary message into all of that?
That's the encoding part of my job.
And the other part, sir?
Getting the messenger to take it away. Shall we try that now?
Thank you, sir. I'll take these straight to the radio room.
Keep them together on the way.
Yes sir. No loose ends.
No loose papers will do.
Sir, they can actually turn this back into words?
The intended recipient can.
And if the enemy gets it?
Then we hope he finds it as unhelpful as you do.
Sir, permission to deliver the encoded message?
Granted. It has spent enough time in this cabin.
Sir, the radioman said he wanted it quickly. That should please him.
His pleasure was not one of the settings on the machine.
No sir. I'll just tell him it's ready.
A sound choice.
Sir, do I get the first message back as well?
Take the papers together. Don't separate the input from the result.
Both of them, sir. Understood.
And neither of them belongs in your locker.
Sir, I was certain I would recognize at least my own name in there.
An unfortunate property for a secret message to have.
Yes sir. I see why that would be a problem.
Good. Give the enemy the same difficulty. Off to the radioman.
Encoding complete, sir. I'll get this sent.
You'll deliver it. The radio watch will get it sent.
Sir, may I fold these to carry them?
You can carry them without putting them in your cap.
I wasn't going to use my cap, sir.
Then we're already making progress. Dismissed.
Sir, does the order of these letters matter very much?
Enough that you shouldn't let anyone helpfully rearrange them.
Yes sir. I'll keep the helpful men away.
Start with yourself. Take it as it is.
Sir, I can't tell whether the news is good or bad now.
That is not a defect in the encoding.
No sir. I wasn't complaining.
Then the radio room is your next stop.
Cleared for transmission, sir. I'll inform the watch officer.
Deliver the encoded message to the radioman first.
Sir, does it say exactly what it said before?
Provided the recipient follows his procedure, yes.
I don't see how, sir.
You don't need to. You need to carry it without changing it.
Sir, could the enemy work this out by guessing?
I would rather we didn't give him time to try. Take it for transmission.
Yes sir. I'll stop guessing myself, then.
That will save some time too.
Sir, the radioman will ask whether you've finished with this.
Tell him I have, and that it is now his turn.
He won't like the second part, sir.
He needn't like it to transmit it.
Sir, should I cover it while I walk back?
You should keep it safe. Encoding isn't an excuse to be careless.
Understood, sir. I'll mind the paper.
That's your part of the operation.
Message encoded, sir. My next stop is the radio watch.
Correct. Carry on.
Sir, this is the first message today I haven't been tempted to read.
What tempted you about the others?
Nothing improper, sir. I was speaking hypothetically.
Then I suggest you leave before we discuss hypothetical charges.
Sir, it looks as though the machine had a disagreement with the alphabet.
The alphabet survived. Take the message to the radioman.
Yes sir. No need to explain the disagreement to him?
There is never a need to explain that sentence to anyone.
Sir, will the officer ashore know who encoded this?
He'll know it came through the proper channel.
I thought you might want the credit, sir.
A message delivered correctly will be sufficient.
Sir, it's all ready. Nothing more for me to wait for?
Nothing here. The radio watch is waiting for you now.
Sir, the words have disappeared but the message is still there?
The words have been encoded. They haven't fallen out of the paper.
Yes sir. That would be rather difficult to carry back.
You seem to have managed a difficult thought already. Off you go.
Sir, I'd offer to help with the next one, but...
But?
I don't believe you need my help with the machine.
Delivering this one will help me with the next. Dismissed.
Sir, this should leave the Western Kingdom scratching its head.
It should reach our own people first. Attend to that part.
Our people first, sir. Understood.
By way of the radioman, please.
Sir, could I explain to the men how you did that?
Could you?
No sir. Not really.
Then we have two good reasons for you not to try.
Sir, I'll be careful with this. It looks important now.
It was important when you brought it in.
Yes sir. I mean it looks officially important.
It is officially ready for the radio room. Move along.
Sir, what should I say when I get there?
Encoded and cleared for transmission.
Encoded and cleared for transmission, sir.
That's it.
It sounded more complicated on the way in.
That was before you had an answer. Dismissed.
Sir, you aren't going to encode it?
Not in its present form. The request has been rejected.
Then I'll take it back for correction, sir.
Good. Don't ask the radioman to make the corrections.
Sir, is your machine out of order?
The machine is fine. The message hasn't been cleared for encoding.
I see, sir. I'll report that accurately.
Please do. The machine has enough work without defending its reputation.
Encoding refused, sir. Understood.
Return the message to the officer who submitted it.
Sir, they said this one was urgent.
They needed to send a proper request urgently, then.
I'll take it straight back, sir.
That is the useful sort of urgency.
Sir, I suppose I can't return with an encoded version of the rejection?
A plain rejection should be clear enough.
Yes sir. I thought it might seem more official.
It is official. Take it back as it is.
Sir, could you encode it and let them fix the paperwork later?
No. Authorization comes before encoding.
Yes sir. I thought I should ask.
You have your answer. Make sure they hear it.
Rejected for encoding, sir. I'll return it.
And make it clear that it is not to be transmitted.
Sir, the radioman has been waiting for this.
Then he needs to know it hasn't been approved.
I expect he'll have something to say, sir.
He may say it to the officer responsible for the request.
Sir, I haven't altered a single word of it.
I didn't say you had. I'm rejecting the message presented to me.
Yes sir. I wanted to be quite clear about my involvement.
Your involvement continues until you've taken it back.
Sir, would it pass if somebody with a higher rank brought it?
The rank of the messenger doesn't repair the request.
That's useful to know, sir.
Use it by delivering the rejection to your superior.
Sir, so there won't be any code for me to carry?
There is a rejected message for you to carry. Take that.
Sir, I could have sworn they checked it before giving it to me.
Then they should have no trouble checking it again.
Yes sir. I'll try not to sound as though that's my suggestion.
The rejection is mine. The suggestion about your tone is your own.
Sir, is this what they mean by a security problem?
This is what I mean by a message that cannot be processed.
I'll use your wording, sir.
A wise precaution. Dismissed.
Sir, the officer won't be pleased that I came back with the same writing.
He can read why it wasn't cleared before submitting it again.
Yes sir. I won't attempt to explain the technical side.
You would both benefit from that restraint.
Sir, should I bring another copy?
Bring a properly authorized message. A second copy alone won't help.
Sir, I thought the encoding would hide whatever was wrong with it.
It is meant to hide the contents from the enemy, not the request from me.
Of course, sir. I had that the wrong way round.
Take the message back before you find another way round the rules.
Sir, perhaps I should wait here until somebody approves it.
Would standing in my doorway improve the authorization?
Probably not, sir.
Then take it to someone who can put it in order.
Sir, are the contents suspicious?
The request has not met the requirements. That is the result to report.
No speculation, sir.
Especially not in the mess.
Sir, am I supposed to take this to the radioman anyway?
To your superior. It hasn't been cleared for transmission.
Sir, I'm beginning to think carrying messages is complicated work.
Only if you try to decide which rules apply to them.
I'll leave that part to you, sir.
And take care of the return journey yourself.
Sir, is there anything I can do to get this encoded?
Return it to its author with the rejection.
I was hoping for something less uncomfortable, sir.
You asked for something useful. Dismissed.
Sir, they'll ask whether I explained how important it was.
Tell them you explained it to someone who understands the regulations.
Yes sir. I don't think they'll ask me to explain it twice.
Let us hope not.
Rejected, sir. Should I keep my voice down when I tell them?
Keep the report private, not inaudible. They need to understand it.
Sir, I could ask the chief to bring it himself.
You could ask him to correct the request instead.
He may choose the first option, sir.
Then I'll have the same conversation with the chief.
Sir, what if the message was already promised to the radio watch?
A promise doesn't clear it for encoding.
No sir. I'll tell them not to expect it yet.
Tell them to expect a corrected request first.
Sir, I shouldn't have told the radioman I'd be back in a minute.
Did you?
I was trying to sound efficient, sir.
How is that working out?
I'll avoid giving him another estimate.
Start by giving him an accurate result.
Sir, may I ask whether you could make an exception?
You may ask. There will be no exception.
I shall report that the question was considered, sir.
You shall report that the message was rejected.
Sir, perhaps they won't notice it hasn't been encoded.
What do you intend to tell them?
That it was rejected, sir. Immediately and in full.
Excellent. I was about to make this a much longer conversation.
Sir, the request is rejected. Does that conclude my visit?
It concludes this one. A corrected message may earn you another.
I'll ask them to get it right before sending me, sir.
Give them the rejected request. That should help.
Sir, I don't think the officer expected STASEC to stop this.
Then the officer has learned something about STASEC.
And I have learned not to make predictions, sir.
You can now demonstrate what you've learned. Return the message.
Incoming message for decoding, sir. The radio watch sent me straight here.
Then you've made the correct number of stops. Let me have it.
Sir, the XO would like to know what this says.
So would whoever went to the trouble of encrypting it, I imagine.
He said you would make sense of it, sir.
Give it here. We'll see what there is to make sense of.
Sir, I was told to bring you this intercept. Is that the right word?
For something the radio watch picked up, yes.
Good. I was rehearsing the report on the way.
The paper will do most of the talking. Hand it over.
Message to decipher, sir. I kept the writing facing inward.
Expecting someone to read the cipher over your shoulder?
I didn't want to find out who could, sir.
A reasonable precaution. Let me see it.
Sir, the radioman says he has done his part with this one.
And now you have come to find out whether I will do mine.
I wouldn't put it quite like that, sir.
No, I expect you wouldn't. The message, please.
Sir, may I leave this with you for decoding?
Put it on the desk where I can see it.
The chief sent me, sir. He says this isn't a job for guessing.
What an encouraging thing for the chief to say.
He was looking at me when he said it.
Even more encouraging. Let me have the message.
